title: Design Playbook
scopeHtml: Scope: Latency budgets, reliability, fallbacks, scale and a framework for design questions.

notes.title: A framework for design questions
notes.html:
The seven-step structure (use it out loud in interviews).

  1. Clarify requirements.
    • Functional: users, tasks, inputs/outputs, languages, tools/actions, citations needed?
    • Non-functional: scale (users, requests/day, peak RPS), latency (TTFT, total), quality bar, availability, cost budget, security/privacy/compliance, residency.
    • Constraints: existing stack, team size, timeline.
  2. Define success metrics. Task success/resolution rate, accuracy/groundedness, latency, cost per task, safety rate, user satisfaction.
  3. Propose the simplest baseline. One prompt? Workflow? RAG? Agent? Justify the choice by predictability, data, risk.
  4. Draw the architecture and data flow. Ingestion, retrieval, generation, post-processing, storage, observability.
  5. Choose models and techniques. Model tiering and routing, API vs self-host, reasoning model or not, caching, structured outputs, fine-tuning only if justified.
  6. Quality, safety and evaluation. Eval set, guardrails, human fallback, red teaming, monitoring.
  7. Operations and trade-offs. Scaling, reliability, cost, rollout, risks, what you'd build later, what you'd measure.

Interview tips. Ask clarifying questions first; state assumptions with numbers; give a baseline then iterate; call out trade-offs explicitly ("I choose X over Y because…"); mention failure modes and mitigation; connect every component to a requirement.

Real life. An architect asks about the family and budget before drawing the house.

notes.title: Latency budgets
notes.html:
Method. Start from the user-facing target (e.g. first token < 1.5 s, total < 8 s for a streamed answer) and allocate a budget to each stage; measure p95, not averages.

Illustrative RAG chat breakdown (TTFT target 1.5 s).

Stage Budget
Network + auth + routing 100 ms
Input guardrails (parallel with next) 100 ms
Query rewrite (small model, optional) 250 ms
Embedding + hybrid search 150 ms
Rerank 150 ms
Prompt assembly 20 ms
LLM time to first token 600 ms
Slack / jitter 130 ms

Reduction techniques. Parallelize independent stages (BM25 + vector, guardrails + retrieval); skip rewriting when unnecessary; smaller models for auxiliary steps; prompt/prefix caching; shorter prompts; speculative decoding; streaming; regional deployment near users; warm instances; precomputation (summaries, embeddings); caching of frequent queries; avoid sequential tool calls where batch endpoints exist.

For agents. Latency = steps × (model + tool). Reduce steps via better tools/batching, parallel calls, plan-and-execute, smaller models for simple steps; show progress; allow async completion.

Real life. Planning a journey with time per leg and a buffer.

notes.title: Scaling
notes.html:
Capacity math. Required tokens/s = RPS × (avg input + avg output) per second. Compare against provider rate limits (RPM/TPM) or per-GPU throughput. Example: 100 RPS peak × 2,500 tokens = 250k tokens/s processed (mostly input); output 100 × 400 = 40k tokens/s — requires large capacity or negotiated limits and prompt caching to cut input cost.

Scaling levers.

  • Horizontal scaling of stateless services behind load balancers; autoscale on queue depth/latency.
  • Rate-limit aware clients: token-bucket per provider key, multiple accounts/regions, adaptive concurrency.
  • Queues and buffering to smooth bursts; priority classes (interactive vs batch).
  • Model tiering (small model handles the bulk).
  • Caching to cut calls.
  • Vector store scaling: sharding, replicas, partitioning by tenant, quantization.
  • Self-hosted inference: more replicas, continuous batching, tensor parallelism, autoscaling with warm pools.
  • Data pipeline scaling: parallel ingestion workers, batch embedding.

What breaks first at 10x. Provider rate limits → cost → vector store memory/latency → tail latency/queueing → observability volume → human review capacity. Plan each.

Real life. Sizing a motorway by rush-hour traffic, not the daily average.

notes.title: Reliability and fallbacks
notes.html:
Design for each failure.

Failure Mitigation
Primary provider outage / 5xx automatic failover to secondary provider/model (portable prompts, tested), or cached/simplified response
Rate limit 429 backoff + jitter, honor retry-after, queue, shift load to batch/secondary key, shed low-priority
Slow responses timeouts with deadline propagation, hedged requests for critical paths, smaller-model fallback
Malformed output validate, retry once with error, repair, fallback
Retrieval failure fall back to keyword search or no-RAG answer with disclaimer, or clarify
Tool failure retries, alternative tool, graceful message, partial results
Guardrail false positive safe refusal with appeal path, human review queue
Stream drop resume/retry, don't persist partial output

Principles. Define SLOs; one retry layer; circuit breakers; idempotency; graceful degradation to a non-AI path; regularly exercise failover; monitor error budgets.

Real life. A spare tyre you have actually checked.

notes.title: Cost trade-offs
notes.html:
Think in unit economics. Cost per request/resolution/user vs value created. Design levers in order of ease and safety: prompt/output trimming → prompt caching → retrieval instead of stuffing → model routing/cascades → batch APIs → distilled/fine-tuned small models → self-hosting at steady volume → hardware optimizations.

Trade-off examples.

  • Reranker adds 150 ms and a little cost but lets you pass 5 chunks instead of 20 (saves prompt tokens): often net positive.
  • Reasoning model improves hard-question accuracy but costs 5 to 20x per query: route only complex queries.
  • Semantic cache saves money but risks wrong answers: restrict to FAQs with strict thresholds.
  • Fine-tuning has upfront cost but removes 3k tokens of few-shot per call: pays back at volume.

Guardrails. Quotas, budgets, anomaly alerts, kill switches, forecasting; tie pricing to usage.

Real life. A shop watching margin per item, not just total sales.

notes.title: Worked example: customer-support assistant
notes.html:
Requirements. 50k conversations/day (peak 40 RPS), answers from the help centre and account data, EU residency, first token < 2 s, escalate to humans, audit trail.

Design.

  1. API layer: authenticated streaming chat endpoint, per-user rate limits, session store.
  2. Intent router (small model): FAQ vs account action vs complaint/escalation vs out-of-scope.
  3. Knowledge path (RAG): hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) over EU-region store, metadata filters (product, locale), cross-encoder rerank, top 5 chunks, "answer only from sources" prompt with citations, mid-size model; prompt caching for the static policy prefix.
  4. Action path: narrow tools (get_order_status, create_return_label) with per-user credentials; confirmation before state-changing actions; idempotency keys.
  5. Guardrails: PII redaction before logs, moderation, injection checks on retrieved/ticket text, output validation; low-confidence → human handoff with transcript summary.
  6. Reliability: provider failover to secondary EU model, timeouts, circuit breakers, degrade to FAQ search if LLM down.
  7. Observability: traces with versions, cost per conversation, groundedness sampling, escalation and CSAT dashboards.
  8. Evaluation: 500-case eval from historical tickets (including unanswerable, adversarial), CI gates, nightly runs, canary releases.
  9. Cost: routing keeps ~70% of traffic on a small model; estimate $0.01 to 0.03 per conversation; budgets per tenant.

Trade-offs discussed. RAG vs fine-tune (RAG for facts), long context vs retrieval (retrieval for scale/permissions), agent vs workflow (workflow with a router; agentic only for complex multi-step cases), build vs buy (managed vector DB initially).

Metrics. Resolution rate, containment, escalation precision, hallucination rate, p95 TTFT, cost per resolution, CSAT.

Real life. A well-run help desk with scripts, specialists and a supervisor for hard cases.

notes.title: Common mistakes
notes.html:
1. Jumping to agents (or multi-agent) when a workflow or single call suffices.
  2. No eval or tiny demo-driven validation.
  3. Ignoring cost until the bill arrives; no per-feature attribution.
  4. Trusting model output without validation; executing output unsafely.
  5. No fallbacks or untested failover.
  6. Unpinned model versions; no prompt versioning.
  7. Weak tenant isolation or permission checks in the prompt instead of retrieval.
  8. Stuffing context instead of retrieving; ignoring lost-in-the-middle.
  9. Skipping guardrails and red teaming.
  10. Treating prompts as static; no feedback loop.
  11. Over-engineering (complex frameworks, too many tools) before proving value.
  12. Ignoring latency tails and rate limits at scale.

Real life. Building a house without checking the foundations.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Framework. Clarify requirements and constraints → success metrics → simplest baseline → architecture/data flow → models and techniques → quality/safety/eval → operations and trade-offs. Think aloud with numbers.

Latency. Budget per stage using p95; parallelize, cache, shrink prompts, tier models, stream; agents multiply steps, so cut steps and show progress.

Scaling. Convert RPS and token sizes into tokens/s, compare with provider limits or GPU throughput; queue and prioritize; rate-limit-aware clients; autoscale; plan what breaks first at 10x.

Reliability. Failover, backoff with jitter and retry-after, circuit breakers, validation and repair, degraded modes, tested drills, SLOs.

Cost. Unit economics; trim, cache, retrieve, route, batch, distil, self-host at volume; evaluate every optimization for quality.

Worked example. Support assistant with router, hybrid RAG + rerank + citations, narrow action tools with confirmation, guardrails, human handoff, failover, observability, evals and canaries, EU residency.

Mistakes to avoid. Agents by default, no evals, unmanaged cost, unvalidated outputs, no fallbacks, unpinned versions, weak isolation, context stuffing, no guardrails/feedback loops, over-engineering.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Start with the simplest thing that could work, and say why."
  • "Budget latency per stage, and show where the big term is."
  • "Every optimization is gated by the eval."
  • "Name the failure modes before the interviewer does."
